tip: 'sabırla' is 'sabır' (patience) + -la: with patience, patiently. Adding -la/-le to a noun turns it into a how adverb.
'güzelce' is 'güzel' + -ce: nicely. Add -ce/-ca to an adjective to make an adverb of manner, how something is done.
'rağmen' (despite) needs the noun before it in the -a/-e form, so 'bu' becomes 'buna': 'buna rağmen' = despite this.
'binmek' takes the -a/-e ending for what you board: 'arabaya bindim' = I got in the car, never 'arabayı bindim'.
'geçerek' is 'geç' + -erek: by crossing. Add -erek/-arak to a verb to show the means, how the main action happened.
'küçükken' is 'küçük' + -ken: when little. Attach -ken to say while or when that state held: 'küçükken' = back when we were small.
'aldığım peynir' means the cheese I bought. The -dığım ending turns a verb into a that-I-did label on the noun after it.
'çatısından' inserts a buffer n: 'çatı' + sı + n + dan. The n slides between the -sı (its) ending and the -dan (from) ending so vowels do not clash.
Comparisons put the yardstick in the -dan/-den (from) form plus 'daha': 'trenden daha yavaş' = slower than the train.
'bırakmışlar' uses -mış for something you did not witness: apparently they left it. It reports or infers rather than states firsthand.
The -iyor ending is the present continuous for what is happening now: 'bekliyorsunuz' = you are waiting, lines up with 'şu anda' = right now.
The -la ending means with and stacks after the my-ending: 'arkadaş' plus -ım (my) plus -la gives 'arkadaşımla' = with my friend.
To say before doing something, put -madan önce on the verb: 'uyumadan önce' = before sleeping.
'yüzünden' means because of and is used for a cause you blame: 'rüzgâr yüzünden' = because of the wind, points at what caused the delay.
The -se ending means if: 'giderseniz' = if you go, setting up the condition for the rest of the sentence.
To say I need to do something, use the verb plus -mem gerekiyor: 'yenilemem gerekiyor' = I need to renew.
'her ihtimale karşı' is a fixed phrase meaning just in case, literally against every possibility.
The -arak ending means by or while doing: 'koşarak' = by running, describing how I got home.
Plurals take -lar after back vowels and -ler after front ones: 'yumurtalar' (eggs) but 'ekmekler' (breads).
An infinitive plus 'için' means in order to: 'almak için' = in order to buy.
Turkish says 'şarkı söylemek', literally to say a song, for to sing: 'şarkı söyledi' = sang.
Add -yle to a noun to say with that feeling: 'öfke' (anger) plus -yle gives 'öfkeyle' = angrily.
The -ce ending turns an adjective into an adverb: 'güzel' (nice) becomes 'güzelce' = nicely.
A specific, known object takes -i: 'haber' becomes 'haberi', marking the news as a definite thing already in mind.
Both nouns get marked in this chain: 'zeytinyağlıların' ends in -ın (of the dishes) and 'kralı' adds -ı pointing back, so 'kralıdır' = their king.
'olmazsa olmazı' is a set phrase for the indispensable part, literally if-it-isn't it-isn't, so 'cacığın olmazsa olmazı' = the must-have of cacik.
'birbiri' means each other, and with -yle it becomes 'birbirleriyle' = with one another.
Put 'en' before an adjective for the superlative, the most: 'en sevdiğim' = the one I love most.
The -çi ending names the person who does something: 'bek' plus -çi gives 'bekçi' (guard), and 'ziyaret' plus -çi gives 'ziyaretçiler' = visitors.
-dan marks from and -ya marks to: 'İstanbul'dan' 'Ankara'ya' = from Istanbul to Ankara.
